description: Catalog of the units in which cloud services are measured and billed. Stable layer: it changes very little over time.

limit_types.name: Pool (pooled quota)
limit_types.explanation: A total you can spend however you like during the period. If the month gives you 180,000 vCPU-seconds, you can spend them on one long request or on a million short ones.
limit_types.why_it_matters: A one-off heavy request breaks nothing as long as the month's total is enough.

limit_types.name: Per-request cap
limit_types.explanation: A maximum that no single request can exceed, no matter how much of the total you have left over.
limit_types.why_it_matters: This is the most important distinction in this entire catalog. An expensive operation (verifying a password, generating a PDF) always fails, even if the whole month is unused.

limit_types.name: Daily cap
limit_types.explanation: A pool that refills every day, usually at midnight UTC.
limit_types.why_it_matters: A traffic spike in a single day can lock you out until the next day, even if the month is going comfortably.

limit_types.name: Concurrency cap
limit_types.explanation: How many things can be happening at the same time, with no limit on the cumulative total.
limit_types.why_it_matters: It limits the peak, not the volume. You notice it at peak hours.

units.name: vCPU-second
units.what_it_measures: One virtual processor core busy for one second.
units.plain_words: It's 'one second of a processor'. If your program uses 2 cores for 3 seconds, you spent 6 vCPU-seconds.
units.handy_equivalent: 180,000 vCPU-seconds per month ≈ one core working for 50 hours, or 60,000 requests of 3 seconds.

units.name: vCPU-hour
units.what_it_measures: One virtual core reserved for one hour, whether it's used or not.
units.plain_words: Like renting an engine by the hour: you pay for having it available, even if it's idle.
units.handy_equivalent: A 2-core machine running all month = ~1,460 vCPU-hours.

units.name: OCPU-hour
units.what_it_measures: An Oracle-specific unit. One OCPU is roughly equivalent to one full physical core, not one thread.
units.plain_words: It's an Oracle vCPU-hour, but each OCPU performs roughly like two vCPUs from other providers.
units.warning: Don't compare OCPUs to vCPUs one to one: you'd underestimate Oracle by a factor of nearly two.
units.handy_equivalent: 1,500 OCPU-hours per month = 2 OCPUs running continuously (a month has ~730 hours).

units.name: GB-second
units.what_it_measures: One gigabyte of memory reserved for one second.
units.plain_words: It combines how much memory you requested with how long you held it. Half the memory for twice as long costs the same.
units.formula: GB of allocated memory × execution seconds
units.handy_equivalent: 400,000 GB-seconds per month ≈ a 512 MB function running for nine days straight.

units.name: GiB-second
units.what_it_measures: Same as the GB-second but with gibibytes (1,024 MiB instead of 1,000 MB).
units.plain_words: The same idea, with a slightly bigger ruler: a GiB is 7.4% larger than a GB.
units.warning: Different providers use GB or GiB for the same thing. Comparing without converting introduces a 7% error.

units.name: CPU milliseconds per request
units.what_it_measures: How long a single request can occupy the processor, from start to finish.
units.plain_words: A stopwatch per visit. If your code takes longer than allowed to think, that visit fails.
units.warning: It doesn't count waiting time (database queries, calls to other APIs): only the actual computation. That's why a slow query doesn't penalize you, but hashing a password does.
units.handy_equivalent: 10 ms is more than enough to assemble a page; it isn't enough to verify a password with PBKDF2 at 100,000 iterations, which costs about 33 ms.

units.name: CPU minutes per day
units.what_it_measures: A daily pool of processing that refills every 24 hours.
units.plain_words: A daily work allowance. Once it runs out, the site stops responding until the next day.
units.handy_equivalent: 60 minutes per day = 3,600 seconds of computation, about 1,200 requests of 3 seconds.

units.name: GPU-hour
units.what_it_measures: One accelerator card reserved for one hour.
units.plain_words: Renting a graphics card to train or run artificial intelligence models.
units.warning: It's the most expensive unit in the catalog, between 10 and 100 times a vCPU-hour. The card model matters as much as the number of hours.

units.name: Request
units.what_it_measures: Every time someone or something asks your service for something.
units.plain_words: A visit, a call, a click that reaches the server. Loading a page usually generates several.
units.warning: A single visit from one person can count as 10 or 20 requests if the page requests images, fonts, and data separately.

units.name: Invocation
units.what_it_measures: Each execution of a function, wherever it comes from.
units.plain_words: Like a request, but counting code starts instead of visits: it includes whatever a timer or a queue triggers.

units.name: Class A operation (write)
units.what_it_measures: Operations that modify or list: uploading, copying, listing contents.
units.plain_words: The 'expensive' operations of file storage.
units.warning: They cost on the order of ten times more than read operations. Listing a folder counts as a write even though you write nothing.

units.name: Class B operation (read)
units.what_it_measures: Operations that only read: downloading a file, checking whether it exists.
units.plain_words: The 'cheap' operations of file storage.

units.name: RU/s (request units per second)
units.what_it_measures: A composite Azure Cosmos DB unit that blends read, write, CPU, and memory into a single number.
units.plain_words: A per-second effort budget for the database. Reading a small document costs ~1 RU; writing it costs ~5.
units.warning: It's reserved up front, not consumed by usage: you pay for the capacity even if nobody uses it.

units.name: Row read
units.what_it_measures: Every row the database had to examine to answer, not the ones it returned.
units.plain_words: If you look for a needle in a haystack with no index, you pay for the whole haystack even though you walk away with one needle.
units.warning: A poorly indexed query can read millions of rows and return one. It's the most common way to exhaust a quota without realizing it.

units.name: Row written
units.what_it_measures: Every row inserted, modified, or deleted.
units.plain_words: Every new or corrected entry in the database.
units.warning: Updating a row that has indexes also counts the updates to those indexes.

units.name: Query
units.what_it_measures: Every instruction sent to the database.
units.plain_words: Every question your program asks the database.
units.warning: Some plans limit how many queries you can make within a single request, not just how many per month.

units.name: LCU (load balancer capacity unit)
units.what_it_measures: A composite AWS unit that blends new connections, active connections, bandwidth, and evaluated rules.
units.plain_words: A made-up number that summarizes how much work you gave the traffic dispatcher.
units.warning: You're billed for the dimension you consume the most, not for the sum. Hard to estimate in advance.

units.name: GB-month
units.what_it_measures: One gigabyte stored for a full month.
units.plain_words: It's not 'how much you store' but 'how much you store for how long'. Ten GB for half a month = 5 GB-months.
units.formula: GB stored × fraction of the month they were there

units.name: GiB (gibibyte)
units.what_it_measures: 1,073,741,824 bytes: 1,024 mebibytes.
units.plain_words: A 'computing gigabyte'. It's 7.4% larger than the commercial gigabyte (1 billion bytes).
units.warning: When one provider says GiB and another says GB for the same product, a direct comparison is off by 7%. Always check which one each uses.

units.name: IOPS (input/output operations per second)
units.what_it_measures: How many individual reads or writes the disk can handle per second.
units.plain_words: How many times per second the disk can serve a request. It matters when there are many small accesses, as in a database.
units.warning: Many cheap disks give 'burstable' IOPS: they perform well for a while and then get throttled.

units.name: MB/s (sustained throughput)
units.what_it_measures: How many megabytes per second it can move continuously.
units.plain_words: The width of the hose. It matters for large files; IOPS matter for small files.

units.name: Minimum retention days
units.what_it_measures: The minimum time you'll be billed for a file, even if you delete it earlier.
units.plain_words: A minimum commitment. If you put something in archive storage with a 90-day minimum and delete it the next day, you pay the 90 days anyway.
units.warning: It's the classic cold storage trap: it looks ten times cheaper until you need to rotate the data.

units.name: Number of objects
units.what_it_measures: How many files are stored, regardless of their size.
units.plain_words: A million tiny files can cost more than one huge file, because each one carries its own record.

units.name: GB out (egress)
units.what_it_measures: Data leaving the provider toward the internet or another region.
units.plain_words: What it costs for your visitors to download your pages, images, and files.
units.warning: It's the most common hidden cost in the entire cloud, and the one that varies most by region: egress from São Paulo can cost six times more than from Virginia. Bringing data in (ingress) is almost always free.
units.handy_equivalent: 1 GB per month ≈ 2,000 visits to a 500 KB text page. It runs out very quickly if you serve images or video.

units.name: GB in (ingress)
units.what_it_measures: Data coming into the provider from outside.
units.plain_words: What your users upload. It's almost always free, precisely so that it's easy for you to get data in and hard to get it out.

units.name: Requests per second
units.what_it_measures: How much simultaneous traffic it can handle before rejecting or queuing.
units.plain_words: The peak it can handle, not the total it processes.

units.name: DNS queries per month
units.what_it_measures: How many times someone asked for your domain's address.
units.plain_words: Every time a new browser looks up where your site lives.

units.name: Email sent
units.what_it_measures: Every message delivered to the recipient's mail server.
units.plain_words: Every email your system sends: confirmations, password recovery, notices.
units.warning: A send to 100 recipients counts as 100, not 1.

units.name: SMS (priced by country)
units.what_it_measures: Each text message, billed according to the destination country and carrier.
units.plain_words: Unlike email, here the price changes radically depending on where you send: there can be twentyfold differences between countries.
units.warning: Never estimate the cost of SMS with a single price: it has to be calculated per destination country.

units.name: Voice minute
units.what_it_measures: Every minute of a call, usually distinguishing inbound from outbound.
units.plain_words: Like the good old phone rate, with a different price depending on the destination.

units.name: Participant-minute
units.what_it_measures: One attendee connected for one minute.
units.plain_words: A meeting of 5 people for 10 minutes is 50 participant-minutes, not 10.
units.warning: Cost grows with the square of the group size in mesh video calls: it's the unit that surprises people most on the bill.

units.name: Push notification
units.what_it_measures: Every alert sent to a mobile device or browser.
units.plain_words: Every time you make someone's phone ring.

units.name: Concurrent connection
units.what_it_measures: How many clients can be connected at the same time on a persistent basis.
units.plain_words: In a chat or a live board, how many people can be watching at the same time.

units.name: Queue message
units.what_it_measures: Every message put into or taken out of a work queue.
units.plain_words: Every task you leave noted down to process later.
units.warning: Putting in and taking out usually count as two separate operations.

units.name: MAU (monthly active user)
units.what_it_measures: How many distinct people used the service at least once in the month.
units.plain_words: It doesn't count how many accounts you have, but how many were used this month.
units.warning: It's the most dangerous pricing unit for a growing product: cost rises with users even if each one does very little.

units.name: Input token
units.what_it_measures: The pieces of text you send to a language model.
units.plain_words: A token is a piece of a word. In Spanish, about 100 tokens equal 70 or 80 words.
units.warning: Input tokens usually cost 3 to 5 times less than output tokens. Counting them together distorts any estimate.

units.name: Output token
units.what_it_measures: The pieces of text the model generates as its response.
units.plain_words: What the model writes. It's the expensive part.

units.name: Processed page
units.what_it_measures: Every page from which text is extracted.
units.plain_words: A photo of a receipt or a sheet of a PDF.
units.warning: A 20-page PDF counts as 20, not 1.

units.name: Character
units.what_it_measures: Every letter, number, or symbol processed.
units.plain_words: The typical unit of machine translation and speech synthesis. A page of text is about 2,000 characters.

units.name: Audio minute
units.what_it_measures: Every minute of recording transcribed or analyzed.
units.plain_words: The length of the recording, not what was said in it.

units.name: Processed image
units.what_it_measures: Every image analyzed, transformed, or generated.
units.plain_words: Every photo the service looks at or creates.

units.name: GB ingested
units.what_it_measures: How much log data entered the observability system.
units.plain_words: The weight of everything your application writes about itself.
units.warning: Logs grow much faster than people expect, and they're billed twice: for ingesting and for retaining.

units.name: Active time series
units.what_it_measures: Every unique combination of metric and labels that received data.
units.plain_words: If you measure 'requests' with a label per country and you have 50 countries, that's 50 series, not one.
units.warning: Adding a label with many possible values (such as the user identifier) can multiply the bill by a thousand. This is called cardinality explosion.

units.name: Span (trace)
units.what_it_measures: Every step recorded within the path of a request.
units.plain_words: A request that passes through five components generates five spans.

units.name: Availability check
units.what_it_measures: Every time a bot checks whether your site responds.
units.plain_words: Checking every minute is ~43,200 checks per month; every five minutes, ~8,640. The interval determines the cost.

units.name: Per-transaction percentage + fixed
units.what_it_measures: A proportional share of the amount plus a fixed amount per operation.
units.plain_words: Typically something like '2.9% + 0.30 USD'. On small charges the fixed part dominates: on a 1 USD charge, the fee can be a third.
units.warning: It's the only unit in the catalog that scales with your revenue and not with your technical consumption.
